questions.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ by inspection.
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{2}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{a}_{2}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{3}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{2}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is spanned by just $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}\}.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -14 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}5 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -14 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ that is to say, 

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

$$

$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\},$ that is to say, 

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

questions.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B=\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=3$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ meaning that

$$
3\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+1\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 1=3.$

\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 14 \\ 2 & -1 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 7 \\ 2 & -1 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ meaning that

$$
2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+(-5)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}14 \\ 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot (-5)=-10.$

questions.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B=\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 8\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -21 \\ -52\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -21 \\ -52\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=-7 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=-21 \\ 7{x}_{1}+8{x}_{3}=-52\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -7 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 & -21 \\ 7 & 0 & 8 & -52\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & 8 & -52\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-4,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=-3,$ meaning that

$$
(-4)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+(-3)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -21 \\ -52\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=(-4)+0+(-3)=-7.$

questions.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B=\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 17\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 17\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=5 \\ 5{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=17\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 5 & 7 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -8 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ meaning that

$$
2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+1\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 17\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 1=2.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/7d5c2f2aaa1ee01159856bcfad7ef1039c169c2fdb96c9c4ab17db5ba9be9067.svg) ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/784f5d018101808c55cf63b332ae50c9d4fc8e3ded23ad9144e417052d2eaba3.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/491d6bb66fd54ae64e406eef6607526c23c6451a3ed0df837d63170c0b9adb95.svg) Find a basis of $S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 15 \\ 2 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ that is to say,

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of a Span
canonical_examples.problem:
The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,$ $\mathbf{a}_2,$ $\mathbf{a}_3,$ and $\mathbf{a}_4$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3, \mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ If that is the case, find $x_1 + x_2 + x_3,$ where $\mathbf{a}_4=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2+x_3\mathbf{a}_3.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/3ff69817bd8aeb5d8326b7ea9fdc68ceeef52840d4f77ee7dffb9f72514f4532.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ So, we want to find $x_1, x_2, x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/79525b86cbbbc191f9a19ffa817fdaebeb0d1f6bd99eb97ce3f642a7fdf6033e.svg)

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=2 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=-2 \\ -3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ -3 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=-5,$ $x_2=0,$ and $x_3=7,$ meaning that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/c732a274f27d98231f9a94dad40ff15f53e82f00b076ba46464ac640c2765703.svg)

Therefore, $x_1 + x_2 +  x_3 = (-5) + 0 + 7 = 2.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of a Span

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/aaa76e82d8d54b305cfcfb0414f1fe7dd4d1c9d3ff932b4206a7b864922b394e.svg)

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/237305d1b82f44e0c365f721a33c35d8d983bd5facd4471d1885e8180ec7267e.svg)
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/1d0ff277adbace09315a1c0cd7c964eac41f5e2f080d0e32f888f379be435da0.svg)

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/79c529aa2fb5373ff9f8798300b1423ea63f90778bd4832ba1276f6af9c21f04.svg)

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}(-{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){a}_{1}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){a}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/aaa76e82d8d54b305cfcfb0414f1fe7dd4d1c9d3ff932b4206a7b864922b394e.svg)

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/237305d1b82f44e0c365f721a33c35d8d983bd5facd4471d1885e8180ec7267e.svg)
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/1d0ff277adbace09315a1c0cd7c964eac41f5e2f080d0e32f888f379be435da0.svg)

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/79c529aa2fb5373ff9f8798300b1423ea63f90778bd4832ba1276f6af9c21f04.svg)

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}(-{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){a}_{1}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){a}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$

tutorials.name: Finding a Basis by Identifying Pivot Columns
tutorials.problem:
In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. But what can we do when it's not so easy to tell? For example, consider the subspace

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/4c12a6e56a6cc7cd72371c59f41b33d8876cf4b98aa40766f0e67ad1bc3a32f7.svg)

To find a subset of linearly independent vectors, we can put the vectors in a matrix and compute the reduced row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent (or redundant) vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

**But watch out!** We need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So, a basis of $U$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ that is to say, 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/1dd0ca9bae9a29dea8fc34ed3d9fc453a1d52c48f1f19a95c2fb16c65cd9c7d8.svg)

tutorials.name: Finding a Particular Linear Combination of Vectors
tutorials.problem:
Earlier, we computed a basis of 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/944c607bf892f0d346df79dfa08e6bfec699e64feac018d40a733be0a5c11041.svg)

The basis that we found was

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/70a26164bd64f6e4483b38a08187cac2e1498df7f9066e2be9a295e7b04459da.svg)

The vector $\mathbf{a}_3$ was not included in the basis. This means that $\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$

Now, what if we want to find the exact linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that yields $\mathbf{a}_3?$ That is to say, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/2a92f6d5b67012d342685436d6ccc0ae1670791a060129b10c7d858cafda7b26.svg)

This is equivalent to a system with the augmented matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/4defcc004e360ec2e87798b158616575f284ae36369c766ee950c20ae06eff0a.svg)

If we reduced this matrix to the *reduced* row echelon form, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/1be8cce3195aa633e76e855eba391dd8d1342cf0f3a19e0302eaf67e2828b909.svg)

Finally, the third column of the *reduced* matrix tells us that $x_1=4$ and $x_2=5,$ meaning that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/cf5185386d46084579b56fc6ad00769c7c5e7a0d2f320be7ccb28aa4961519ae.svg)

**Watch out!** The matrix must be written in *reduced* row echelon form (with $1$'s for pivots and $0$'s above and below the pivots), not just row echelon form.

tutorials.title: Finding a Particular Linear Combination of Vectors
tutorials.content:
Earlier, we computed a basis of 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/944c607bf892f0d346df79dfa08e6bfec699e64feac018d40a733be0a5c11041.svg)

The basis that we found was

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/70a26164bd64f6e4483b38a08187cac2e1498df7f9066e2be9a295e7b04459da.svg)

The vector $\mathbf{a}_3$ was not included in the basis. This means that $\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$

Now, what if we want to find the exact linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that yields $\mathbf{a}_3?$ That is to say, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/2a92f6d5b67012d342685436d6ccc0ae1670791a060129b10c7d858cafda7b26.svg)

This is equivalent to a system with the augmented matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/4defcc004e360ec2e87798b158616575f284ae36369c766ee950c20ae06eff0a.svg)

If we reduced this matrix to the *reduced* row echelon form, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/1be8cce3195aa633e76e855eba391dd8d1342cf0f3a19e0302eaf67e2828b909.svg)

Finally, the third column of the *reduced* matrix tells us that $x_1=4$ and $x_2=5,$ meaning that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274531/assets/cf5185386d46084579b56fc6ad00769c7c5e7a0d2f320be7ccb28aa4961519ae.svg)

**Watch out!** The matrix must be written in *reduced* row echelon form (with $1$'s for pivots and $0$'s above and below the pivots), not just row echelon form.
